title: The Mystery of Coal
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how coal forms, from peat bogs and swamp muck through burial, pressure and heat into lignite, bituminous and anthracite coal, and graphite as the final stage. They describe coal's Carboniferous-period origins (Pennsylvanian epoch, Appalachian region), the "white rot" fungus theory for why coal deposition dropped off, and scientists' counterarguments. They discuss coal as a carbon sink in the carbon cycle, its role in climate change compared with volcanic emissions, and close with a listener mail from Jackson in Canberra, Australia about the show's title and can openers.

segments.title: Opening banter and episode title
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode title 'The Mystery of Coal' and tease that coal's formation is interesting and has been used by humans for a long time.

segments.title: Peat bogs and swamp muck
segments.summary: Coal begins in peat bogs and swamps, where stagnant, oxygen-poor water preserves fallen plant matter and carbon is locked in the muck instead of decomposing as it would on land.

segments.title: Burial, pressure, and coalification
segments.summary: As lakes fill in and swamps become dry land, layers of earth compress the peat. Heat and pressure transform it through coalification, and deeper burial yields different types of coal, with diamonds also starting as swamp muck.

segments.title: Types of coal: lignite, bituminous, anthracite, graphite
segments.summary: The hosts describe lignite as brownish and crumbly, bituminous as the most widely used coal, anthracite as the hardest and cleanest-burning, and graphite as the final stage, which is hard to ignite. They also compare coal and oil formation, which differ mainly by location and source material.

segments.title: Carboniferous period and the Appalachian coal seams
segments.summary: Coal formed mainly in the Carboniferous period, a warm and wet era. Tectonic collisions of Laurasia and Gondwana formed mountains that became the Appalachians, carrying coal-bearing swamp deposits with them.

segments.title: The coal mystery and the white rot theory
segments.summary: Most of the world's coal was deposited in the Pennsylvanian epoch, then deposition dropped off. Giant plants and lignin are discussed, and the white rot theory proposes that a lignin-decomposing fungus appeared near the end of the Carboniferous, which the U.S. Department of Energy supported with genome analysis.

segments.title: Counterarguments to the white rot theory
segments.summary: Some scientists argue that something could already break down lignin before white rot fungi appeared, citing partially decayed fossil plants. An alternative is that tectonic activity caused an unusual spike in coal deposition rather than a sudden drop-off.

segments.title: Coal in the carbon cycle and climate change
segments.summary: Coal acts as a carbon sink that stores carbon underground. Burning it releases carbon far faster than natural processes, and human emissions far exceed volcanic emissions, contributing to global warming and related effects.

segments.title: Listener mail: Jackson from Canberra
segments.summary: A listener from Australia writes about the show's title and says he learned how to use a can opener from the show's podcast, with the hosts joking about can openers.
